title: Predictive processing
content_html:
Predictive processing

In predictive processing (PP) under the Free-Energy Principle (FEP), the brain is a hierarchical generative model. It keeps internal predictions close to incoming sensations by minimizing variational free energy (an upper bound on surprise). In that loop, memory is (i) the model’s learned parameters/priors, (ii) precision (uncertainty) estimates guiding attention, and (iii) cached trajectories (episodic traces/replay) used to predict and plan—so perception, learning, action, and memory are different stances of the same predictive mechanism.

Perception ≈ inference. Feedback predictions flow down; feedforward “errors” flow up. Perception is precision-weighted error minimization to infer hidden causes.

Learning ≈ model update. Parameters/priors are tuned to shrink future prediction error—free energy—over longer timescales (active inference formalizes the full perception–action–learning cycle).

Memory ≈ predictive resource. Hippocampus provides a predictive map; replay selectively accesses past episodes to plan future actions (prioritized memory access).

Predictive-coding architecture/microcircuits: brains cache intermediate results to make inference/planning efficient.

Free-Energy Principle (FEP)

The FEP says any self-organising system that persists (e.g., an organism) must, on average, keep its sensory states within a limited, unsurprising range. Formally, it does this by minimizing variational free energy under a probabilistic generative model of the world. Perception, learning, action — and by extension memory — are just different ways the system updates its beliefs, parameters, and policies to keep expected surprise low over time. In predictive-coding style message passing, descending predictions meet ascending signals and only precision-weighted mismatches (“prediction errors”) drive updates. Learning tunes parameters and precisions across timescales; on this view memory = learned parameters/priors + precision estimates + cached trajectories used to predict/plan.

FEP connects to physics by assuming organisms occupy non-equilibrium steady-states (NESS): their states fluctuate within bounds rather than dissipate. A Markov blanket (sensory & active states) statistically separates internal from external states, defining what can be sensed or influenced. Under mild assumptions, internal states come to encode a probability density over external states — the “inference machine” picture. Risk + Ambiguity seek outcomes close to preferences (low risk) and reduce uncertainty in outcome mappings (low ambiguity). Extrinsic + Epistemic value pursue goals while seeking information (expected information gain/curiosity). This unifies exploitation and exploration under one objective.

FEP is a principle (like least action) constraining viable models of persistent, self-organising systems; specific active-inference models are the testable bits. It’s** not** a claim that organisms literally minimize thermodynamic free energy; here “free energy” is variational, though modern summaries also explain links to physics.

Living systems are open, driven, and far from equilibrium, yet their state-distributions are stationary over relevant timescales: probability mass stays concentrated in a narrow region while energy/entropy continually flow. The organism resists dispersion by shaping beliefs, parameters, and policies so typical trajectories remain inside the high-probability set that defines its phenotype.
